Sub:  Submission of voting results pursuant to Regulation 44 of the SEBI (Listing 
Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015, as amended (‘SEBI 
Listing Regulations, 2015’) 
 
In continuation to our letter dated 9 October 2026 in relation to issuance of Notice of 
Extraordinary General Meeting (‘EGM’) of the Company, this is to inform you that the said 
meeting was held on Monday, 2 November 2026 at 12.45 p.m. (IST) through Video Conference 
(VC) / Other Audio-Visual Means (OAVM) (hereinafter referred to as ‘EGM’) in accordance with 
the applicable provisions of the Companies Act, 2013 ('the Act'), SEBI Listing Regulations, 
2015 and circulars issued by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA), to transact the 
businesses as stated in the Notice convening the EGM.  
 
As per the requirements under SEBI Listing Regulations, 2015 and applicable provisions of the 
Act, please find enclosed herewith the following:  
 
• 
Scrutinizer’s Report dated 3 November 2026, pursuant to Section 108 of the Act and 
Rule 20 of the Companies (Management and Administration) Rules, 2014; and  
• 
Voting results pursuant to Regulation 44(3) of the SEBI Listing Regulations, 2015. 
 
A copy of the same is also being placed on the Company's website and on the website of 
KFin Technologies Limited (E-voting service provider).  
 
Kindly acknowledge and take the same on record. 
 
Thanking you,  
Yours faithfully, 
For BAJAJ FINANCE LIMITED

TCS Enterprise AI Study: 84% say productivity is AI’s top benefit; just 10% let AI act 
without human oversight 
 
25-country global survey shows that security, risk and governance is the #1 factor that leaders are 
considering when deploying AI 
 
MUMBAI, November 04, 2026: Eighty-four percent of executives surveyed rank productivity improvement 
as the leading source of value realized from AI investments, yet only 10% of global enterprises allow AI agents 
to execute decisions without human approval across multiple functions or business areas, according to a new 
global study from Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) (BSE: 532540, NSE: TCS), a global leader in IT services, 
consulting, and business solutions. The study also finds that just 9% of executives report AI agents capable of 
securely orchestrating workflows across enterprise applications. The findings highlight the gap between the 
value that enterprises are already deriving from AI-assisted work and their readiness to give AI agents greater 
autonomy and authority to act. 
 
The study, TCS Enterprise AI Study: Intelligence that is Real, highlights security as a defining factor in the next 
phase of enterprise AI. Security, risk, and governance considerations rank as the leading factor shaping how 
and where AI systems are developed and deployed, ahead of cost, speed, and ease of deployment. That 
emphasis is becoming increasingly consequential as enterprises give AI greater access to applications, 
workflows and decision-making processes. 
 
The findings reflect the evolution toward a Human+AI operating model, where AI progresses from assisting 
employees to taking on greater responsibility and, where appropriate, operating with increasing levels of 
autonomy. As enterprises move along that continuum, deriving greater value from AI will depend on having 
the right security, governance and controls in place to determine where human oversight remains essential 
and where AI can be given greater authority to act. 
 
Amit Kapur, Chief AI and Services Transformation Officer, TCS, said, “We are seeing significant progress in 
scaling AI for enterprises. The shift is clearly in AI moving from assisting people to taking more autonomous 
action with deep access into an enterprise. Productivity is clearly where enterprises are seeing the greatest 
value from AI today, with 84% of executives ranking it as the leading source of value from their AI investments 
though 10% have also indicated that they have seen an uplift in revenue. What seems to be holding 
organisations back – and rightly so – are concerns around security, governance, and resilience. Deploying AI 
responsibly, with the right guardrails and enterprise controls will be the big focus in the next stage of this 
journey.” 
 
Platform independence: Executives are also increasingly focused on AI resilience and flexibility. Ninety 
percent of respondents say that model independence is an important factor in AI investment decisions, while 
34% identify AI sovereignty-related requirements involving control over data location, model choice, and 
compliance as a high or very high organisational risk. The concern is particularly acute in Europe, where 43% 
of respondents cite AI sovereignty-related requirements as a high or very high organizational risk. At the 
same time, only 7% of global respondents report having organization-wide provider-switching continuity 
plans, suggesting that concern about model dependence and sovereignty is advancing faster than operational 
preparedness. 
 
Other key global findings from the report include: 
• 
AI economics are under review: 39% of enterprises said that they continue to assess whether AI 

Page 2 of 3 
 
initiatives generate sufficient value relative to token and compute costs.  
• 
Enterprise knowledge remains fragmented: 44% of respondents report that important business 
knowledge remains embedded within employees or fragmented documentation, potentially 
limiting AI's ability to consistently access enterprise context.  
• 
Open-source AI is gaining traction: 46% report targeted deployment of open-source AI for 
selected use cases.  
• 
AI's workforce impact is becoming less predictable. The proportion of leaders saying it is still 
too early to determine AI's effect on jobs rose from 4% in 2024 to 19% in 2026.  
• 
Productivity remains the leading source of AI value, followed by improvements in customer 
experience and the development of new products or services. 
 
Regional AI Priorities and Readiness Vary: The study also identified notable regional differences in enterprise 
AI adoption. North America showed particular strength across several enterprise AI foundations, with 15% 
of respondents reporting that AI is treated as a strategic enterprise capability. Europe showed a strong focus 
on AI sovereignty, with 43% citing sovereignty-related requirements as a high or very high organizational risk. 
Meanwhile, the UK and Ireland stood out on operational resilience, reporting comparatively strong levels of 
AI continuity planning and governance integration. 
 
Survey methodology: The study surveyed 1,333 senior business and technology leaders across 25 countries 
and 12 industries. Respondents included C-suite executives, divisional leaders, and senior vice presidents and 
vice presidents from organizations with annual revenues ranging from US$500 million to more than US$20 
billion. 
 
The full report, TCS Enterprise AI Study: Intelligence that is Real, is available at: TCS Enterprise AI Study: 
Intelligence that is real 
 
 
About Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) 
Tata Consultancy Services (BSE: 532540, NSE: TCS) is the technology partner of choice for industry-leading 
organizations worldwide. Since its inception in 1968, TCS has upheld the highest standards of innovation, 
engineering excellence, and customer service. 
 
It has set an aspiration to become the world's largest AI-led technology services company and is enabling its 
clients to transform themselves across the full AI stack, from infrastructure to intelligence. 
 
Rooted in the heritage of the Tata Group, TCS is focused on creating long term value for its clients, its 
investors, its employees, and the community at large. With a highly skilled workforce spread across 56 
countries and 194 service delivery centers across the world, the company has been recognized as a top 
employer in six continents. With the ability to rapidly apply and scale new technologies, the company has 
built long-term partnerships with its clients. Many of these relationships have endured into decades and 
navigated every technology cycle, from mainframes in the 1970s to artificial intelligence today. 
 
TCS sponsors 14 of the world’s most prestigious marathons and endurance events, including the TCS New 
York City Marathon, TCS London Marathon, Tata Mumbai Marathon, and TCS Sydney Marathon with a focus 
on promoting health, sustainability, and community empowerment. 
 
TCS generated consolidated revenues of over US $30 billion in the fiscal year ended March 31, 2026.  For

more information, visit www.tcs.com 
 
Follow TCS on LinkedIn| Instagram | YouTube| X

Grasim and Suzlon enter into pact to Develop, Commercialize and Scale India’s 
first Wind Turbines with Recyclable Blades Powered by Recyclamine® 
Technology. 
4 November 2026 | New Delhi 
Grasim Industries Limited’s Advanced Materials Division and its renewable arm Aditya 
Birla Renewables Limited (ABRen) have entered into a Memorandum of 
Understanding (MoU) with Suzlon Energy Limited, to collaborate on a pilot basis for 
the development, commercialization, and scaling of wind turbines equipped with 
recyclable blade technology. Signed at the Bharat Renewable Energy Summit & Expo 
2026, the partnership is founded on a shared commitment to advancing circularity in 
the wind energy sector and accelerating the adoption of sustainable end-of-life 
solutions for wind turbine blades. 
Today, conventional wind turbine blades are predominantly manufactured using 
thermoset composite materials that are difficult to recycle at the end of their service 
life, often resulting in landfill disposal or incineration. Blades manufactured using 
Recyclamine® epoxy technology, supplied by Grasim, can be chemically recycled at 
end-of-life, enabling the recovery of valuable composite constituents for reuse in new 
applications. This breakthrough technology supports circular economy principles, 
minimizes waste, reduces environmental impact, and enhances the overall 
sustainability of wind energy projects. 
Under this collaboration, Suzlon, as the wind turbine OEM, will integrate Recyclamine® 
technology into the manufacturing of recyclable wind turbine blades. Aditya Birla 
Renewables will deploy a wind turbine equipped with recyclable blades at one of its 
selected project sites, demonstrating the commercial viability of circular blade 
technology under real-world operating conditions. The parties will also jointly explore 
opportunities to drive broader commercialization and market adoption of recyclable 
blade-enabled wind turbines powered by Recyclamine® technology across India and 
other mutually agreed markets. 
“This collaboration marks an important step toward building a truly circular wind energy 
ecosystem. By combining the Recyclamine® technology with Suzlon’s manufacturing 
expertise and ABRen’s renewable energy ambitions, we are demonstrating that 
sustainability and innovation can go hand in hand. Together, we aim to accelerate the 
adoption of recyclable wind turbine blades and set new benchmarks for resource 
efficiency in the wind industry", said Rajesh Balakrishnan, Chief Executive Officer, 
Advanced Materials, Grasim Industries Ltd. 

 
 
 
 
 
                           
 
“The future of renewable energy lies not just in generating clean power, but in building 
truly circular solutions. At Suzlon, we are advancing this vision through our flagship 
S144 platform, which has one of the world's lowest carbon footprints among wind 
turbines, and by working towards making all future turbines recyclable within the next 
three to four years. This partnership brings together innovation and scale to accelerate 
material circularity, with the potential to enable significant CO₂ savings. It is another 
step towards ensuring that every turbine we build delivers lasting value for both the 
planet and future generations." Said Girish Tanti, Co-Founder, Suzlon Group. 
“At ABRen, we believe the energy transition must be accompanied by innovation that 
enhances environmental sustainability. This partnership is an important step toward 
addressing the end-of-life challenges associated with wind turbine blades and 
advancing circularity within the renewable energy sector.” said Amit Jain, Chief 
Executive Officer, Aditya Birla Renewables Limited 
 
About Grasim Industries Limited 
 
Grasim Industries Limited, a flagship company of the Aditya Birla Group, ranks 
amongst the top publicly listed companies in India. Incorporated in 1947, it started as 
a textiles manufacturer in India. Today, it has evolved into a leading diversified 
player with leadership presence across many sectors. It is a leading global producer 
of Cellulosic Fibres, Diversified Chemicals, Fashion Yarn and Fabrics producer in 
India. Implementing next phase of transformational growth journey, the Company 
has entered paints business under the brand name ‘Birla Opus’ and launched ‘Birla 
Pivot’, the B2B online marketplace for building materials. Through its subsidiaries, 
UltraTech Cement, Aditya Birla Capital and Aditya Birla Renewables, it is also India’s 
prominent cement producer, leading diversified financial services player and clean 
energy solutions player. 
Grasim’s Advanced Materials business focuses on innovative, high-performance, 
and sustainable solutions, including bio-based, waterborne, and recyclable epoxy 
technologies. Visit- www.grasim.com 
 
 
Aditya Birla Renewables Limited (ABRen), subsidiary of Grasim Industries Ltd, is 
a leading integrated clean energy platform, with capacity over 4.4 GWp across 60+ 
projects in 12+ states. 
 
About Suzlon Energy Limited 
At Suzlon Group, we believe energy enables human progress, and the new world of 
energy will be powered by Good Energies That Work. With revenues of USD 1.75+ 
billion for FY26 and market capitalization of USD 5.6+ billion as of September 30, 
2026, we are constantly advancing the good energies that make the new world work 

 
 
 
 
 
                           
 
by building clean, dependable, intelligent, integrated, and affordable energy 
ecosystems for a rapidly electrifying world. With ~22+ GW of wind energy capacity 
installed across 17 countries and a diverse portfolio of renewable energy businesses, 
Suzlon today is a wind-first full-stack renewable energy solutions conglomerate with 
businesses spanning across RE Technology (Wind+Solar+Storage), RE Development 
Company, RE Projects, and RE Asset Management. For over three decades, Suzlon 
has partnered with leading PSUs, IPPs, and C&I businesses as a lifetime renewable 
energy partner. Our next-generation product portfolio includes 2.x MW, 3.x MW, 5.x 
MW and 6.x MW wind turbine systems alongside integrated renewable energy 
solutions built for the new world of energy. Headquartered at Suzlon One Earth in 
Pune, India, the Suzlon Group (NSE: SUZLON, BSE: 532667) comprises RE Tech: 
Wind | Storage | Solar, RE DevCo, RE Projects, RE AMS, and its subsidiaries.

Grasim and Suzlon enter into pact to Develop, Commercialize and Scale India’s 
first Wind Turbines with Recyclable Blades Powered by Recyclamine® 
Technology. 
4 November 2026 | New Delhi 
Grasim Industries Limited’s Advanced Materials Division and its renewable arm Aditya 
Birla Renewables Limited (ABRen) have entered into a Memorandum of 
Understanding (MoU) with Suzlon Energy Limited, to collaborate on a pilot basis for 
the development, commercialization, and scaling of wind turbines equipped with 
recyclable blade technology. Signed at the Bharat Renewable Energy Summit & Expo 
2026, the partnership is founded on a shared commitment to advancing circularity in 
the wind energy sector and accelerating the adoption of sustainable end-of-life 
solutions for wind turbine blades. 
Today, conventional wind turbine blades are predominantly manufactured using 
thermoset composite materials that are difficult to recycle at the end of their service 
life, often resulting in landfill disposal or incineration. Blades manufactured using 
Recyclamine® epoxy technology, supplied by Grasim, can be chemically recycled at 
end-of-life, enabling the recovery of valuable composite constituents for reuse in new 
applications. This breakthrough technology supports circular economy principles, 
minimizes waste, reduces environmental impact, and enhances the overall 
sustainability of wind energy projects. 
Under this collaboration, Suzlon, as the wind turbine OEM, will integrate Recyclamine® 
technology into the manufacturing of recyclable wind turbine blades. Aditya Birla 
Renewables will deploy a wind turbine equipped with recyclable blades at one of its 
selected project sites, demonstrating the commercial viability of circular blade 
technology under real-world operating conditions. The parties will also jointly explore 
opportunities to drive broader commercialization and market adoption of recyclable 
blade-enabled wind turbines powered by Recyclamine® technology across India and 
other mutually agreed markets. 
“This collaboration marks an important step toward building a truly circular wind energy 
ecosystem. By combining the Recyclamine® technology with Suzlon’s manufacturing 
expertise and ABRen’s renewable energy ambitions, we are demonstrating that 
sustainability and innovation can go hand in hand. Together, we aim to accelerate the 
adoption of recyclable wind turbine blades and set new benchmarks for resource 
efficiency in the wind industry", said Rajesh Balakrishnan, Chief Executive Officer, 
Advanced Materials, Grasim Industries Ltd. 

 
 
 
 
 
                           
 
“The future of renewable energy lies not just in generating clean power, but in building 
truly circular solutions. At Suzlon, we are advancing this vision through our flagship 
S144 platform, which has one of the world's lowest carbon footprints among wind 
turbines, and by working towards making all future turbines recyclable within the next 
three to four years. This partnership brings together innovation and scale to accelerate 
material circularity, with the potential to enable significant CO₂ savings. It is another 
step towards ensuring that every turbine we build delivers lasting value for both the 
planet and future generations." Said Girish Tanti, Co-Founder, Suzlon Group. 
“At ABRen, we believe the energy transition must be accompanied by innovation that 
enhances environmental sustainability. This partnership is an important step toward 
addressing the end-of-life challenges associated with wind turbine blades and 
advancing circularity within the renewable energy sector.” said Amit Jain, Chief 
Executive Officer, Aditya Birla Renewables Limited 
 
About Grasim Industries Limited 
 
Grasim Industries Limited, a flagship company of the Aditya Birla Group, ranks 
amongst the top publicly listed companies in India. Incorporated in 1947, it started as 
a textiles manufacturer in India. Today, it has evolved into a leading diversified 
player with leadership presence across many sectors. It is a leading global producer 
of Cellulosic Fibres, Diversified Chemicals, Fashion Yarn and Fabrics producer in 
India. Implementing next phase of transformational growth journey, the Company 
has entered paints business under the brand name ‘Birla Opus’ and launched ‘Birla 
Pivot’, the B2B online marketplace for building materials. Through its subsidiaries, 
UltraTech Cement, Aditya Birla Capital and Aditya Birla Renewables, it is also India’s 
prominent cement producer, leading diversified financial services player and clean 
energy solutions player. 
Grasim’s Advanced Materials business focuses on innovative, high-performance, 
and sustainable solutions, including bio-based, waterborne, and recyclable epoxy 
technologies. Visit- www.grasim.com 
 
 
Aditya Birla Renewables Limited (ABRen), subsidiary of Grasim Industries Ltd, is 
a leading integrated clean energy platform, with capacity over 4.4 GWp across 60+ 
projects in 12+ states. 
 
About Suzlon Energy Limited 
At Suzlon Group, we believe energy enables human progress, and the new world of 
energy will be powered by Good Energies That Work. With revenues of USD 1.75+ 
billion for FY26 and market capitalization of USD 5.6+ billion as of September 30, 
2026, we are constantly advancing the good energies that make the new world work 

 
 
 
 
 
                           
 
by building clean, dependable, intelligent, integrated, and affordable energy 
ecosystems for a rapidly electrifying world. With ~22+ GW of wind energy capacity 
installed across 17 countries and a diverse portfolio of renewable energy businesses, 
Suzlon today is a wind-first full-stack renewable energy solutions conglomerate with 
businesses spanning across RE Technology (Wind+Solar+Storage), RE Development 
Company, RE Projects, and RE Asset Management. For over three decades, Suzlon 
has partnered with leading PSUs, IPPs, and C&I businesses as a lifetime renewable 
energy partner. Our next-generation product portfolio includes 2.x MW, 3.x MW, 5.x 
MW and 6.x MW wind turbine systems alongside integrated renewable energy 
solutions built for the new world of energy. Headquartered at Suzlon One Earth in 
Pune, India, the Suzlon Group (NSE: SUZLON, BSE: 532667) comprises RE Tech: 
Wind | Storage | Solar, RE DevCo, RE Projects, RE AMS, and its subsidiaries.

Q3 & 9M CY2026 Earnings Conference Call Transcript 
October 30, 2026 
 
 
Moderator: 
Ladies and gentlemen, good day, and welcome to Varun Beverages Limited's 
Earnings Conference Call.  
I now hand the conference over to Mr. Anoop Poojari from CDR India. Thank you, 
and over to you, Mr. Poojari. 
Anoop Poojari: 
Thank you. Good afternoon, everyone, and thank you for joining us on Varun 
Beverages Q3 CY2026 earnings conference call. We have with us Mr. Varun 
Jaipuria, Executive Vice Chairman and Whole-Time Director, and Mr. Raj Gandhi, 
President and Whole-Time Director of the company. Mr. Ravi Jaipuria, Chairman of 
the company, has had to excuse himself from today's call due to personal reasons. 
We will begin the call with opening remarks from the management, following which 
we will have the forum open for a question-and-answer session. Before we proceed, 
I would like to point out that some statements made in today's call may be forward-
looking in nature, and a disclaimer to this effect has been included in the results 
presentation shared with you earlier. 
I will now request Mr. Varun Jaipuria to make his opening remarks. 
Varun Jaipuria: 
Good afternoon, everyone, and thank you for joining us on our earnings conference 
call. I hope you have had a good chance to review our results presentation for the 
third quarter and nine months ended September 30, 2026.  
We are pleased to report a strong performance in the third quarter of CY2026. 
Consolidated sales volume revenue grew 28.7% with a volume growth of 22.5% in 
India and 39.9% in international markets. Revenue from operations increased by 
33.2% year-on-year to Rs. 66,075.6 million, while EBITDA grew 25.1% to Rs. 
14,267.1 million. Higher packaging costs weighed on margins during the quarter, 

 
Page 2 of 21 
 
although improved realizations and operating leverage from strong volume growth 
helped partially offset these pressures.  
In India, we continue to witness healthy volume growth during the quarter, extending 
the positive trend seen since May. This performance was supported by our extensive 
distribution network, expanded manufacturing capacities and ongoing investments 
in chilling infrastructure. We also saw improved realizations supported by growth in 
higher-value categories such as dairy and the introduction of premium offerings 
including ‘Ad Rush’ and the ‘Evervess’ mixers range. 
Our international business continued to make strong progress during the quarter with 
Africa remaining a key continent for expansion. With effect from 1st August 2026, 
the merger of Twizza with BevCo has been completed, and we expect to unlock 
significant operational synergies in the coming quarters. During the quarter, we have 
also started beverage operations in Kenya and introduced two new beverage brands, 
‘BOLT UP’ and ‘XTREME FIZZ’, marking another step towards strengthening our 
footprint in the fast-growing African region. We also entered into an exclusive 
distribution agreement with Mondelez in Zimbabwe, further broadening our product 
offering in the market. 
We are also taking measured steps towards diversifying our business into adjacent 
categories. The incorporation of KIVA Spirits and Company Limited marks an 
important step in exploring opportunities in ready-to-drink beverages, alcoholic 
beverages and allied products. Our approach will remain focused on pursuing 
opportunities that leverage our execution capabilities and offer attractive long-term 
growth potential.  
In line with our dividend policy, the Board of Directors have approved an interim 
dividend of 25% of the face value, Rs. 0.50 per share, resulting in total cash outflow 
of Rs. 1,691 million. 
Looking ahead, our focus will remain on driving growth across our existing markets, 
supported by investments we have already made over the recent years. Alongside 
this, we will selectively pursue opportunities to broaden our business while 
maintaining a clear emphasis on profitability and long-term value creation. 
I would now like to invite Mr. Gandhi to share the key highlights of our operational 
and financial performance. Thank you. 

 
Page 3 of 21 
 
Raj Gandhi: 
Thank you, Mr. Vice Chairman. Good afternoon, and a warm welcome to everyone 
joining us today. Let me take you through the financial and operational performance 
of the third quarter and nine months ended 30th September 2026. 
Revenue from operations net of excise duty and GST increased by 33.2% year-on-
year to the level of Rs. 66,076 million in Q3 CY2026. For 9M CY2026, revenue grew 
by 23.3% to the level of Rs. 218,146 million. Growth during the quarter was primarily 
driven by a 28.7% increase in consolidated sales volume to the level of 354.4 million 
cases in India. Volume grew by a strong 22.5% during the quarter, while international 
territories recorded robust growth of 39.9%. 
Consolidated net realization per case for beverages improved by 2.2% year-on-year, 
supported by a 0.5% increase in India on account of growth in high-value categories 
and further launch of premium categories like Ad Rush, Evervess mixers range, 
calibrated discounting and efficient price-pack architecture. 
In international markets, realization per case improved on account of improved 
realization in South Africa and foreign exchange impact. In terms of volume mix, 
carbonated soft drinks accounted for 73.3%, juice-based drinks for 4.8% and 
packaged drinking water for 21.9% of total sales volume during the quarter. 
Coming to margins, gross margin moderated by 334 basis points year-on-year to 
53.1% in Q3 calendar year 2026, primarily due to higher packaging material costs, 
including preforms, shrink films, closures, cans, arising from geopolitical disruptions. 
However, packaging cost contributed approximately 300 bps of pressure on gross 
margin. In addition, sales of non-beverage products such as preforms and caps in 
India increased by approximately 104% during the quarter. Given their higher COGS, 
these products had an impact of approximately 100 basis points on gross margin in 
India.  
The impact of around a 16% increase in sugar price was largely offset by a higher 
proportion of low sugar and no sugar products in India with their share increasing 
from 44% levels in the corresponding Q3 of 2025 to the level of 88% in the Q3 of the 
2026 in India, almost double. This is after accounting for the sharing of sugar 
reduction benefits with PepsiCo through concentrate cost as part of the transition to 
a low sugar portfolio. 
EBITDA increased by 25.1% year-on-year to the level of Rs. 14,267 million in Q3 
CY2026 with EBITDA margin at 21.6%. The margin moderated only by 140 basis 
points in spite of higher material costs year-on-year, primarily due to the contraction 
in gross margin, primarily offset by operating leverage from robust volume growth 

 
Page 4 of 21 
 
across India and international territories. Importantly, despite the supply chain 
disruptions and input cost pressures arising from geopolitical developments, EBITDA 
margins in India remained broadly stable on a year-to-year basis during 9M CY2026.  
PAT increased by 13.5% year-on-year to the level of Rs. 8,306 million in Q3 CY2026, 
compared with the Rs. 7,315 million in the corresponding quarter last year. 
Depreciation and finance costs increased by 34.5% and 53.5%, respectively, 
primarily on account of acquisition of Twizza in South Africa and the associated debt 
funding. Other income declined by 18.8%, reflecting relatively stable currency 
movements during the quarter.  
For 9M CY2026, EBITDA increased by 19.9% to the level of Rs. 52,746 million, while 
PAT grew up by 15.5% to Rs. 32,023 million. 
Looking ahead, we are encouraged by the strong volume growth, delivered across 
India and international markets. Our endeavor will be to sustain healthy growth over 
the longer term, supported by effective utilization of our expanded capacities and 
market infrastructure. At the same time, we will remain focused on managing input 
costs and improving operating efficiencies to support profitability as we scale our 
operations. 
On that note, I will come to an end of our opening remarks and would like to now ask 
the moderator to open the forum for any questions or suggestions that you may have. 
Thank you. 
Moderator: 
Thank you very much, sir. Ladies and gentlemen, we will now begin with the 
question-and-answer session. The first question is from the line of Abneesh Roy from 
Nuvama. Please go ahead. 
Abneesh Roy: 
Thanks and congrats on strong volume growth in India and overseas also. My first 
question is on the gross margins. What will be the outlook for next quarter and if 
possible, even the March quarter? And coming specifically to this quarter, earlier the 
information sharing was that sugar that change has happened. So very low sugar 
usage is there in terms of the portfolio, plus in terms of the packaging, a lot of the 
buying has been done for the September quarter. I wanted to understand where 
things change versus that initial comment. And on your specific comment that non-

that? And could you bifurcate how much is the packaging increase, sugar increase 
and this non-beverage increase? That can give us more clarity. Thank you. 

 
Page 5 of 21 
 
Raj Gandhi: 
Abneesh, in the opening remarks, we clarified that food costs have not had a 
significant impact due to the change in our portfolio and innovation. The share of low-
sugar or no-sugar products has increased from 44% to 88%, which has been 
managed very well. However, due to geopolitical factors, packaging costs have 
increased. Your comment is correct, but that was relevant only until the war started, 
around 28th February. At that time, we had stated that we were fully covered for the 
next quarter. As you might have noticed, there was no impact on gross margins last 
quarter. 
However, all purchases going forward were at higher prices. We had not stocked 
inventory for a period longer than the 2nd quarter, which helped us manage the 
previous quarters. However, prices are now definitely higher. 
Abneesh Roy: 
And how do we see outlook? 
Raj Gandhi: 
Outlook, this is a macro factor impacting both food and packaging costs. However, 
in our case, through innovation, we have been able to manage sugar costs quite 
well. As far as material costs are concerned, it may not be possible to comment

However, in terms of mitigating the 3%-4% impact in gross margins, we have already

Varun Jaipuria: 
Abneesh, looking at the geopolitical situation, nobody really knows when this war is

Raj Gandhi: 
Abneesh, just to add to what Mr. Varun Jaipuria stated, we have already reduced the

Abneesh Roy: 
Thanks. Just one quick follow-up. So this is extreme geopolitical situation, which

Varun Jaipuria:

Abneesh Roy: 
Sure. Second and last question on this Mondelez relationship in Africa in Zimbabwe.

Africa from Mondelez? 
Varun Jaipuria: 
It is very nascent. Mondelez is one of the best brands you can work with. And we are 
very fortunate to partner up with them. They already have an existing business of 
about $11 million in Zimbabwe with the local partner they were working with, We are 
sure he was not able to harness the full potential of the market. Hence, we are 
partnering up with them. We do understand Zimbabwe very well, it was a greenfield 
project for us a few years back. At present, we have got a very high market share

Moderator:

Hi, good afternoon. A couple of questions. First is on the competition side. You know,

So what I am saying is like Tata Consumer on their conference call mentioned that

evolving. What is your view on the competition in general, your latest thoughts,

Raj Gandhi: 
Vivek, instead of giving a forward statement, we draw your attention to look at this

Varun Jaipuria: 
See, Vivek, one more thing to add. If you remove the raw material pressure, there is

President and Whole-Time Director of the company. Mr. Ravi Jaipuria, Chairman of 
the company, has had to excuse himself from today's call due to personal reasons. 
We will begin the call with opening remarks from the management, following which 
we will have the forum open for a question-and-answer session. Before we proceed, 
I would like to point out that some statements made in today's call may be forward-
looking in nature, and a disclaimer to this effect has been included in the results 
presentation shared with you earlier.

Varun Jaipuria: 
Good afternoon, everyone, and thank you for joining us on our earnings conference 
call. I hope you have had a good chance to review our results presentation for the 
third quarter and nine months ended September 30, 2026.  
We are pleased to report a strong performance in the third quarter of CY2026. 
Consolidated sales volume revenue grew 28.7% with a volume growth of 22.5% in 
India and 39.9% in international markets. Revenue from operations increased by 
33.2% year-on-year to Rs. 66,075.6 million, while EBITDA grew 25.1% to Rs. 
14,267.1 million. Higher packaging costs weighed on margins during the quarter, 

 
Page 2 of 21 
 
although improved realizations and operating leverage from strong volume growth 
helped partially offset these pressures.  
In India, we continue to witness healthy volume growth during the quarter, extending 
the positive trend seen since May. This performance was supported by our extensive 
distribution network, expanded manufacturing capacities and ongoing investments 
in chilling infrastructure. We also saw improved realizations supported by growth in 
higher-value categories such as dairy and the introduction of premium offerings 
including ‘Ad Rush’ and the ‘Evervess’ mixers range. 
Our international business continued to make strong progress during the quarter with 
Africa remaining a key continent for expansion. With effect from 1st August 2026, 
the merger of Twizza with BevCo has been completed, and we expect to unlock 
significant operational synergies in the coming quarters. During the quarter, we have 
also started beverage operations in Kenya and introduced two new beverage brands, 
‘BOLT UP’ and ‘XTREME FIZZ’, marking another step towards strengthening our 
footprint in the fast-growing African region. We also entered into an exclusive 
distribution agreement with Mondelez in Zimbabwe, further broadening our product 
offering in the market. 
We are also taking measured steps towards diversifying our business into adjacent 
categories. The incorporation of KIVA Spirits and Company Limited marks an 
important step in exploring opportunities in ready-to-drink beverages, alcoholic 
beverages and allied products. Our approach will remain focused on pursuing 
opportunities that leverage our execution capabilities and offer attractive long-term 
growth potential.  
In line with our dividend policy, the Board of Directors have approved an interim 
dividend of 25% of the face value, Rs. 0.50 per share, resulting in total cash outflow 
of Rs. 1,691 million. 
Looking ahead, our focus will remain on driving growth across our existing markets, 
supported by investments we have already made over the recent years. Alongside 
this, we will selectively pursue opportunities to broaden our business while 
maintaining a clear emphasis on profitability and long-term value creation. 
I would now like to invite Mr. Gandhi to share the key highlights of our operational 
and financial performance. Thank you. 

 
Page 3 of 21

joining us today. Let me take you through the financial and operational performance 
of the third quarter and nine months ended 30th September 2026. 
Revenue from operations net of excise duty and GST increased by 33.2% year-on-
year to the level of Rs. 66,076 million in Q3 CY2026. For 9M CY2026, revenue grew 
by 23.3% to the level of Rs. 218,146 million. Growth during the quarter was primarily 
driven by a 28.7% increase in consolidated sales volume to the level of 354.4 million 
cases in India. Volume grew by a strong 22.5% during the quarter, while international 
territories recorded robust growth of 39.9%. 
Consolidated net realization per case for beverages improved by 2.2% year-on-year, 
supported by a 0.5% increase in India on account of growth in high-value categories 
and further launch of premium categories like Ad Rush, Evervess mixers range, 
calibrated discounting and efficient price-pack architecture. 
In international markets, realization per case improved on account of improved 
realization in South Africa and foreign exchange impact. In terms of volume mix, 
carbonated soft drinks accounted for 73.3%, juice-based drinks for 4.8% and 
packaged drinking water for 21.9% of total sales volume during the quarter. 
Coming to margins, gross margin moderated by 334 basis points year-on-year to 
53.1% in Q3 calendar year 2026, primarily due to higher packaging material costs, 
including preforms, shrink films, closures, cans, arising from geopolitical disruptions. 
However, packaging cost contributed approximately 300 bps of pressure on gross 
margin. In addition, sales of non-beverage products such as preforms and caps in 
India increased by approximately 104% during the quarter. Given their higher COGS, 
these products had an impact of approximately 100 basis points on gross margin in 
India.  
The impact of around a 16% increase in sugar price was largely offset by a higher 
proportion of low sugar and no sugar products in India with their share increasing 
from 44% levels in the corresponding Q3 of 2025 to the level of 88% in the Q3 of the 
2026 in India, almost double. This is after accounting for the sharing of sugar 
reduction benefits with PepsiCo through concentrate cost as part of the transition to

EBITDA increased by 25.1% year-on-year to the level of Rs. 14,267 million in Q3

points in spite of higher material costs year-on-year, primarily due to the contraction 
in gross margin, primarily offset by operating leverage from robust volume growth 

 
Page 4 of 21

disruptions and input cost pressures arising from geopolitical developments, EBITDA 
margins in India remained broadly stable on a year-to-year basis during 9M CY2026.  
PAT increased by 13.5% year-on-year to the level of Rs. 8,306 million in Q3 CY2026, 
compared with the Rs. 7,315 million in the corresponding quarter last year. 
Depreciation and finance costs increased by 34.5% and 53.5%, respectively, 
primarily on account of acquisition of Twizza in South Africa and the associated debt 
funding. Other income declined by 18.8%, reflecting relatively stable currency 
movements during the quarter.  
For 9M CY2026, EBITDA increased by 19.9% to the level of Rs. 52,746 million, while 
PAT grew up by 15.5% to Rs. 32,023 million.

Letter from the Founders 
Dear Shareholders, 
Last quarter we told you that India has not bought its glasses yet. It is only fair to tell you what kind of company it will 
take to change that. We believe it needs four things this industry never had. It will be an engineering company first, 
because the hardest problems in eyewear, the eye test above all, will not be solved by hiring or spending more. It will 
own its supply chain end to end, to make a ₹500 pair profitably and give it the experience of a ₹50,000 one. It will build 
brands for everyone, from a first pair to the one someone has always wanted. And it will never believe its customers 
are satisfied enough; it will innovate continuously and keep surprising them. That is the company we are building. It is 
easier said than done: it has to push harder, think like founders and builders, and change as fast as the world. 
If one word holds all four, it is evolve. We named our new concept store Lenskart evolv for that reason. It opened in 
Worli, Mumbai, on a belief that the future of eyewear will be shaped not just by what we make but by how people 
discover it. It brings design, culture and technology into one immersive space, the first expression of what an eyewear 
destination, and the Lenskart brand, can be. Walk in, spend an hour, and you will get a flavour of the culture we are 
building and the bar we hold ourselves to: raising the standard, refusing the status quo, thinking from first principles. 
Now, the quarter. Revenue grew 32.5% YoY to ₹2,845 Cr, EBITDA grew to ₹624 Cr (₹392 Cr pre-IndAS, up 65.0%), and 
PAT grew 2.1x to ₹232 Cr. 80 lakh eye tests globally; India SSSG 20.8%. H1 revenue: ₹5,559 Cr, up 33.0%, EBITDA ₹1,213 
Cr (₹753 Cr pre-IndAS), and PAT ₹461 Cr, 87% of full year of FY26. Over the trailing 12 months, revenue crossed ₹10,000 
Cr, EBITDA ₹2,200 Cr (₹1,300 Cr pre-IndAS) and PAT almost ₹800 Cr. Measure us over years, not quarters.  
We have said too little about Hustlr Club: a face scan on the app, a colour, and a complete pair, frame, lenses and 
warranty, for ₹500. Hundreds of thousands did this quarter. It is how we hope the next 100 million Indians find us. A 
year ago, AI at Lenskart meant choosing store locations. Today it runs through the company: it screens every hire, 
trains every new Lenskartian before they meet a customer, answers our customer calls with no IVR and no queue, and 
decides which frame goes to which store. Thousands of store associates start the day with Saathi, our self-learning 
AI assistant. B, our smart glasses, is in 500 stores and online; 90% of buyers took it with a prescription. 
What all this is for. In India, the next curve is 100 million pairs a year, from 32 million today. Affordability, access and 
awareness stand in the way; Hustlr Club answers the first, the eye test the other two, and 100 million pairs needs 80 
million tests. Remote optometry, now in 934 stores, let us open 94 Tier 2+ stores this quarter, a store a day. Our AI-
assisted eye-test now has a name, Drysh: you do most of it yourself, with an optometrist supervising, so each stands 
behind many more tests. Hyderabad, built for 50 million pairs a year, is around twelve months away. 
In the world, International grew 29.5%, with a second straight quarter above 10% EBITDA (pre-IndAS) margin. We 
continue to build a global brand for the next generation of consumers. Meller opens its next experience store on Via

Factory to Face: The Path to 25% 
Shareholders and analysts ask us one question more than any other: how does Lenskart reach a 25% EBITDA 
(pre-IndAS 116) margin? This section is our answer: why we believe the business is built for it, and why we are in 
no hurry to get there. 
Our margin comes from one thing above all: how much of the chain we own, factory to face. 
Seven things decide the profit on a pair of glasses: who owns the brand, who makes the frame, who makes the 
lens, who edges and fits the pair, who sells it, who does the R&D on materials, process and design, and how the 
whole operation is run. In a conventional process, as in most categories, the first five sit with five different 
companies, a brand, a frame maker, a lens maker, a fitter and a retailer, and each keeps a slice of the price.  
Each can only ever improve its own slice, and when a pair needs fixing, no one is answerable to the customer for 
the whole of it. The last two, the R&D that only pays when you own the whole chain, and the way the company 
itself is run, belong to no one in that chain. 
Lenskart chose to own all seven: the brands on the temple, owned or held under exclusive licence for our 
markets; the frame, moulded in our own plants; the lens, surfaced and coated in our own labs; the fitting, done 
centrally; our own R&D in materials, process and design; the store, app and home eye test, with no third-party 
retailer between; and a company run on its own systems and data.  
We did not do it for margin. We did it so that one party answers to the customer for the whole pair, a single throat 
to choke, and so that what we learn from every pair goes into the next. It is also why a ₹500 pair and a ₹50,000 
pair come out of the same factory with the same quality standards. But each of the seven is also a pool of profit, 
and owning all of them lets us work on the whole system rather than one slice.

traditionally done by hand in a shop. We do it centrally and largely by machine at ~75% automation; fitting, quality 
control and packaging are still largely manual. Scale is the biggest lever, because much of the cost here is fixed. 
On top of it sit automation, robotics and utilization, process redesign, and pre-making the most common pairs 
in bulk because the data tells us what will be ordered. Hyderabad, built for 50 Mn pairs a year under one roof and 
twelve months from commissioning, takes all of this to the next level.

large part of same-store growth flows through: India rent fell to 5.7% of revenue from 6.1%, with SSSG of 20.8% 
well ahead of ~5% annual escalations.

customers actually need. Air frames weigh almost nothing and do not break. A great deal of R&D sits behind that, 
and it is why customers pay a premium for them, for the comfort and the innovation. The same is true of our IP 
collections - Masaba, Shantanu & Nikhil, Batman and Superman among them: each takes a great deal of R&D, 
which is why we created Lenskart Studio for them, and why it commands a premium.  Night-drive lenses went 
from lab to store in months; myopia-management lenses for children are a category we are building. B put a 
camera, a speaker and an AI assistant into a prescription pair. We have only just started, but we believe this can 
become one of the largest generators of value in the company. 
Own tech-first operating model. The seventh pool is not a hand in the chain; it is how we run the other six. Being 
an engineering company at heart, we built the entire technology and operating system that runs them in-house, 
so each part talks to the next without a seam. Our stores run on our own point of sale; our eye-test machines run 
our own software. Stores are opened and replenished on our own systems; their people are interviewed by our 
own AI. An order is made just in time in a central factory, surfacing, edging and quality control, on a warehouse 
and factory system we built; delivered on our own logistics software, built to reach the remotest parts of India 
fast, reliably and at the lowest cost; supported afterwards on our own tech; and the customer relationship now 
runs on our own AI. Each system has its own builder, team and its own name: Argus for replenishment, GeoIQ for 
store location, Tango Eye for the floor, Drysh for the eye test, NexS for the factory. 
None of this is static. A large engineering team evolves it constantly, now with AI giving them ten times the reach, 
and we keep bringing more into the fold: CRM came in-house this year; so did IVR and call handling, outsourced 
for years; talent acquisition, interviewing and performance management came in because talent and culture 
matter more now than ever; and Owndays and International are moving onto the same platform.  
How we run all of this decides not only how fast we can scale but what margin we earn in the long term. A company 
can make 100 million pairs a year and run 10,000 stores the old way, a layer of people for every layer of work, with 
cost that grows with the network, or on data and AI from the start, with cost that grows far slower than revenue. 
We believe that in an AI world, the company that uses it fully will find profit pools deeper than the industry has 
seen. 
Every pool we deepen makes the others worth more. That is the case for 25% in the long term.

We want to invest more in marketing, in right places and for the long term; in building Bharat, where most of the 
next 100 million pairs will come from; in scaling International while the unit economics play out. So, we will not 
optimize for reaching 25% as fast as we can. We will optimize for what we set out to do: vision for a billion people, 
and a company that makes a difference for decades. The margin follows the mission, not the other way round.

read margins over years, not quarters. The number might move; the direction will not.

Letter from the Founders 
Dear Shareholders, 
Last quarter we told you that India has not bought its glasses yet. It is only fair to tell you what kind of company it will 
take to change that. We believe it needs four things this industry never had. It will be an engineering company first, 
because the hardest problems in eyewear, the eye test above all, will not be solved by hiring or spending more. It will 
own its supply chain end to end, to make a ₹500 pair profitably and give it the experience of a ₹50,000 one. It will build 
brands for everyone, from a first pair to the one someone has always wanted. And it will never believe its customers 
are satisfied enough; it will innovate continuously and keep surprising them. That is the company we are building. It is 
easier said than done: it has to push harder, think like founders and builders, and change as fast as the world. 
If one word holds all four, it is evolve. We named our new concept store Lenskart evolv for that reason. It opened in 
Worli, Mumbai, on a belief that the future of eyewear will be shaped not just by what we make but by how people 
discover it. It brings design, culture and technology into one immersive space, the first expression of what an eyewear 
destination, and the Lenskart brand, can be. Walk in, spend an hour, and you will get a flavour of the culture we are 
building and the bar we hold ourselves to: raising the standard, refusing the status quo, thinking from first principles. 
Now, the quarter. Revenue grew 32.5% YoY to ₹2,845 Cr, EBITDA grew to ₹624 Cr (₹392 Cr pre-IndAS, up 65.0%), and 
PAT grew 2.1x to ₹232 Cr. 80 lakh eye tests globally; India SSSG 20.8%. H1 revenue: ₹5,559 Cr, up 33.0%, EBITDA ₹1,213 
Cr (₹753 Cr pre-IndAS), and PAT ₹461 Cr, 87% of full year of FY26. Over the trailing 12 months, revenue crossed ₹10,000 
Cr, EBITDA ₹2,200 Cr (₹1,300 Cr pre-IndAS) and PAT almost ₹800 Cr. Measure us over years, not quarters.  
We have said too little about Hustlr Club: a face scan on the app, a colour, and a complete pair, frame, lenses and 
warranty, for ₹500. Hundreds of thousands did this quarter. It is how we hope the next 100 million Indians find us. A 
year ago, AI at Lenskart meant choosing store locations. Today it runs through the company: it screens every hire, 
trains every new Lenskartian before they meet a customer, answers our customer calls with no IVR and no queue, and 
decides which frame goes to which store. Thousands of store associates start the day with Saathi, our self-learning 
AI assistant. B, our smart glasses, is in 500 stores and online; 90% of buyers took it with a prescription. 
What all this is for. In India, the next curve is 100 million pairs a year, from 32 million today. Affordability, access and 
awareness stand in the way; Hustlr Club answers the first, the eye test the other two, and 100 million pairs needs 80 
million tests. Remote optometry, now in 934 stores, let us open 94 Tier 2+ stores this quarter, a store a day. Our AI-
assisted eye-test now has a name, Drysh: you do most of it yourself, with an optometrist supervising, so each stands 
behind many more tests. Hyderabad, built for 50 million pairs a year, is around twelve months away. 
In the world, International grew 29.5%, with a second straight quarter above 10% EBITDA (pre-IndAS) margin. We 
continue to build a global brand for the next generation of consumers. Meller opens its next experience store on Via 
del Corso, Rome, in November. Our brands are learning to speak culture: John Jacobs with Shantanu & Nikhil and 
Masaba; Shunya, inspired by Indian music; and Meller with Diwali edition of its sunglasses for India. 
Where we were tested. Product margin held at 70.0% through a year of the Rupee falling against the RMB. Our teams 
answered with 72% more frames and 52% more lenses from our own plants; that absorbed the currency, and that 
resilience is what we are building. Marketing fell to 4.5% of India revenue, not all of it efficiency; we want to deploy 
more and are waiting for opportunities that build the brand for years, not a quarter. Holding our standard at a store a 
day is hard: NPS had dipped to 77.6 in June and is back at 79.6; that recovery, on a ship this size, is what we are 
proudest of.  
Last quarter we invited you to walk with us in Drishti ki Daud. You walked 800 Mn steps, 15 times round the Earth, and 
30,000 underprivileged people got the glasses they needed. Thank you. Also this quarter, NSE Sustainability Ratings  
rated Lenskart as an ESG Leader with a score of 73 for FY2026. The goal is a way off; we will get things wrong, learn, 
but not move off it. What we have is full clarity of purpose. Thank you for building the future with us.  It is still Day Zero. 
- Peyush Bansal

Factory to Face: The Path to 25% 
Shareholders and analysts ask us one question more than any other: how does Lenskart reach a 25% EBITDA 
(pre-IndAS 116) margin? This section is our answer: why we believe the business is built for it, and why we are in 
no hurry to get there. 
Our margin comes from one thing above all: how much of the chain we own, factory to face. 
Seven things decide the profit on a pair of glasses: who owns the brand, who makes the frame, who makes the 
lens, who edges and fits the pair, who sells it, who does the R&D on materials, process and design, and how the 
whole operation is run. In a conventional process, as in most categories, the first five sit with five different 
companies, a brand, a frame maker, a lens maker, a fitter and a retailer, and each keeps a slice of the price.  
Each can only ever improve its own slice, and when a pair needs fixing, no one is answerable to the customer for 
the whole of it. The last two, the R&D that only pays when you own the whole chain, and the way the company 
itself is run, belong to no one in that chain. 
Lenskart chose to own all seven: the brands on the temple, owned or held under exclusive licence for our 
markets; the frame, moulded in our own plants; the lens, surfaced and coated in our own labs; the fitting, done 
centrally; our own R&D in materials, process and design; the store, app and home eye test, with no third-party 
retailer between; and a company run on its own systems and data.  
We did not do it for margin. We did it so that one party answers to the customer for the whole pair, a single throat 
to choke, and so that what we learn from every pair goes into the next. It is also why a ₹500 pair and a ₹50,000 
pair come out of the same factory with the same quality standards. But each of the seven is also a pool of profit, 
and owning all of them lets us work on the whole system rather than one slice. 
The table on the next page shows where each pool stands, what moved in the last twelve months, and what is 
still ahead.

Own brands. Most frames we sell carry a brand we own, built in-house like Vincent Chase, John Jacobs, Air, 
Hustlr and Hooper, or acquired like Owndays and Meller, so the brand’s share of the price stays in the house. 
Licensed collections are mostly exclusive to our markets and designed and made by us; we control inventory, 
pricing and margin, and the licence fee is the only slice that leaves. The house has lens brands too, and part of 
this quarter’s 6.9% rise in India ASP came from customers choosing Owndays premium lenses. Ahead: more 
brands owned, acquired or exclusively licensed, and more specialized, IP-led products. 
Own frame manufacturing. Baofeng Framekart in China since 2017, Manesar and Bhiwadi since 2021, a 50% joint 
venture with Sunrise in Thailand this year. Every frame moulded in India no longer moves with the dollar. Beneath 
the design sit the moulds, the tooling, the raw material, the process and the plating; each is a layer where 
someone else’s margin, and often someone else’s currency, used to sit. Owning the mould and the process was 
the first layer. Tooling and plating come next, more of it in India, and as volumes grow the mould cost per piece 
keeps falling. 
Own lens manufacturing. We make lenses where precision adds value: progressives, complex powers and 
premium coatings, including Owndays premium lenses, now a significant share of what we sell in India. Behind 
every lens sit the raw materials, the processes, the tooling and the coatings, each with room to improve. Ahead: 
more made in India, more markets served from India, and contact and myopia-management lenses at scale. 
 
 
 
Own edging and fitting. Every pair is made to measure, a dozen steps from eye-test machine to fitted pair, 
traditionally done by hand in a shop. We do it centrally and largely by machine at ~75% automation; fitting, quality 
control and packaging are still largely manual. Scale is the biggest lever, because much of the cost here is fixed. 
On top of it sit automation, robotics and utilization, process redesign, and pre-making the most common pairs 
in bulk because the data tells us what will be ordered. Hyderabad, built for 50 Mn pairs a year under one roof and 
twelve months from commissioning, takes all of this to the next level. 
Own channels. The retailer’s margin is ours; the customer relationship is ours, and so is every eye test on record. 
That record trains our technology and shows us the bottlenecks to efficient scale; remote optometry, which took 
one optometrist’s reach to 934 stores, came out of exactly that. A store’s team and rent are largely fixed, so a 
large part of same-store growth flows through: India rent fell to 5.7% of revenue from 6.1%, with SSSG of 20.8% 
well ahead of ~5% annual escalations.  
Own R&D and innovation. Because we own the first five, we have stretched, over the last few years, into product 
R&D: the material science of frames and lenses, coatings, progressive lens design, process and mould design, 

 
Page 8 of 25 
and for B the hardware, software and firmware. Being direct to the customer, each is designed around what 
customers actually need. Air frames weigh almost nothing and do not break. A great deal of R&D sits behind that, 
and it is why customers pay a premium for them, for the comfort and the innovation. The same is true of our IP 
collections - Masaba, Shantanu & Nikhil, Batman and Superman among them: each takes a great deal of R&D, 
which is why we created Lenskart Studio for them, and why it commands a premium.  Night-drive lenses went 
from lab to store in months; myopia-management lenses for children are a category we are building. B put a 
camera, a speaker and an AI assistant into a prescription pair. We have only just started, but we believe this can 
become one of the largest generators of value in the company. 
Own tech-first operating model. The seventh pool is not a hand in the chain; it is how we run the other six. Being 
an engineering company at heart, we built the entire technology and operating system that runs them in-house, 
so each part talks to the next without a seam. Our stores run on our own point of sale; our eye-test machines run 
our own software. Stores are opened and replenished on our own systems; their people are interviewed by our 
own AI. An order is made just in time in a central factory, surfacing, edging and quality control, on a warehouse 
and factory system we built; delivered on our own logistics software, built to reach the remotest parts of India 
fast, reliably and at the lowest cost; supported afterwards on our own tech; and the customer relationship now 
runs on our own AI. Each system has its own builder, team and its own name: Argus for replenishment, GeoIQ for 
store location, Tango Eye for the floor, Drysh for the eye test, NexS for the factory. 
None of this is static. A large engineering team evolves it constantly, now with AI giving them ten times the reach, 
and we keep bringing more into the fold: CRM came in-house this year; so did IVR and call handling, outsourced 
for years; talent acquisition, interviewing and performance management came in because talent and culture 
matter more now than ever; and Owndays and International are moving onto the same platform.  
How we run all of this decides not only how fast we can scale but what margin we earn in the long term. A company 
can make 100 million pairs a year and run 10,000 stores the old way, a layer of people for every layer of work, with 
cost that grows with the network, or on data and AI from the start, with cost that grows far slower than revenue. 
We believe that in an AI world, the company that uses it fully will find profit pools deeper than the industry has 
seen. 
Every pool we deepen makes the others worth more. That is the case for 25% in the long term. 
Growth first. We have a very small share of India’s eyewear market and low single digits abroad, except 
Singapore, where we hold about a quarter by volume. We have harvested only part of these pools, and 25% is not 
a near-term target. Profitability is running ahead of where we expected: EBITDA (pre-IndAS 116) margin reached 
13.8% from 11.1%, India 16.0% from 13.4%, International 10.6% from 7.3%, even as we opened 165 stores and 
absorbed the currency. We intend to use that room.  
We want to invest more in marketing, in right places and for the long term; in building Bharat, where most of the 
next 100 million pairs will come from; in scaling International while the unit economics play out. So, we will not 
optimize for reaching 25% as fast as we can. We will optimize for what we set out to do: vision for a billion people, 
and a company that makes a difference for decades. The margin follows the mission, not the other way round. 
What could slow it. Currency, until more pairs are made in India; Hyderabad, which carries fixed cost before 
volume; International openings, where costs run ahead of revenue for a period; and campaigns to get Bharat to 
try us for the first time. So, we will not put a timeframe on 25% or lock ourselves to a short-term number when 
the goal now is growth: the first 100 million Indians, and scale in International as the unit economics play out. We 
read margins over years, not quarters. The number might move; the direction will not.

1. Discuss the performance of the India business in Q2. 
India revenue grew 35.3% YoY to ₹1,668 Cr in Q2 FY27. SSSG of 20.8% was broad-based: Metro, Tier 1 and Tier 2+ 
all grew. SPSG, at 27.1%, runs ~6 percentage points ahead of SSSG - once again, demonstrating that adding 
stores to a pincode adds demand rather than dividing it.  
H1 FY27 revenue was ₹3,199 Cr, up 33.0% YoY. 
Five things drove this, and each feeds the others: (A) a widening eye-test funnel; (B) volume growth across 
categories; (C) a deepening customer franchise anchored by Gold; (D) higher ASPs led by premium lenses; (E) 
expanding omnichannel network. 
Eye tests: 70 Lakh eye tests in Q2, up 44.1% YoY. That is how much of India’s demand is still untapped. Stores 
enabled with remote optometry tripled in the last one year – now present in 934 stores, bringing consistent, high 
quality testing to every store and letting each optometrist serve many more customers. 
Volume: Eyewear units grew 26.5% YoY to 85.5 Lakh. Growth was healthy across prescription eyeglasses, 
progressives and contact lenses, and sunglasses grew strongly as customers found far more collections to 
choose from, led by Meller. Volume remains the metric we track religiously: growth led by units  is what keeps 
the quality of growth robust.  
Customer franchise: Quarterly Transacting Customer Accounts grew 18.5% YoY to 46 Lakh. Lenskart Gold 
crossed one crore active members - 103 Lakh at quarter-end, up 38.6% YoY and Q2 subscription fees collections 
were ₹73 Cr, up 54.6%.  
As we flagged in our last letter, Q1 saw a minor dip in NPS; that has reversed, with India NPS back at 79.6 in Q2 
from 77.6 in Q1. 
ASP: India ASP grew 6.9% YoY to ₹1,950, as more customers chose premium lenses - Owndays, Rodenstock, 
Tokai - and progressives took a larger share of the mix. This is happening along with the growing share of Hustlr, 
which is still early. 
Network and omnichannel: 143 net new stores in Q2 (vs 133 in Q2 FY26) and 259 in H1 FY27, taking us to 2,868 
stores across 665 cities. 94 of the Q2 additions were in Tier 2+ towns and we entered 61 new cities - deeper into 
India, while still densifying metros and Tier 1. Digitally influenced sales reached 57% of India revenue, from 50%

This quarter, India continued to showcase margin expansion. EBITDA (pre-IndAS 116) reached ₹267 Cr, up 61.5% 
YoY, with margin at 16.0% (vs 13.4% in Q2 FY26). EBITDA margin reached 21.7% (vs 19.5% in Q2 FY26), with EBITDA 
of ₹362 Cr, up 50.5% YoY.  
Product Margin was 64.0% (vs 63.4% in Q2 FY26), despite the continued appreciation of the RMB against the 
Rupee. The structural investments we have made over the past few years - increased in-house manufacturing 
of frames and lenses, and centralised manufacturing - are helping us sustain this margin, and we continue to 
work very hard to offset the currency headwind. In this quarter, most of the product-margin improvement we 
earned was consumed by currency headwinds.

the Lenskart brand and our house of brands over the long term, rather than transactional spend.

Income Statement Highlights – Q2 FY2027 
❖ Gross Profit was up 15.4% at INR 57,774 Mn from INR 50,066 Mn in Q2 FY2026, with a gross margin of 
74.2%. 
❖ Personnel cost was 18.3% of sales at INR 14,236 Mn compared to INR 11,056 Mn in Q2 FY2026. 
❖ Manufacturing and other expenses were 31.3% of sales at INR 24,381 Mn compared to INR 19,796 Mn in 
Q2 FY2026. 
❖ PBT at INR 15,796 Mn was 20.3% of sales, down 21.3% YoY from INR 20,070 Mn in Q2 FY2026. 
❖ Investment in R&D for the quarter was INR 6,181 Mn (7.9% of sales). 
Balance Sheet Highlights 
❖ Operating working capital was INR 75,420 Mn as on September 30, 2026. Operating days for quarter is at 
87 days. 
❖ Capital Expenditure for the quarter was INR 2,230 Mn. 
❖ Net Debt as on September 30, 2026, stands at INR -33,490 Mn.  
❖ Net Debt Equity as on September 30, 2026, stands at -0.14. 
 
Mr. Nilesh Gupta, Managing Director, Lupin Limited said "We delivered a strong first half of FY27, underpinned by 
solid growth across key markets and sustained profitability. While we remain mindful of near-term challenges, we 
are confident in our long-term growth prospects, supported by the strength of our portfolio, continued 
investments in R&D and commercial capabilities, and our unwavering focus on disciplined execution."

The Company received 4 ANDA and 1 NDA 505(b)(2) approvals from the U.S. FDA, and launched 1 product in the

FY2026.

Pharmaceutical Market (IQVIA MAT September 2026). 
 
Other Developed Markets

accounting for 11% of Lupin’s global sales.

for 4% of Lupin’s global sales.

for Q2 FY2026.

consumers globally, the company enjoys a strong position in India and the U.S. across multiple therapy areas, 
including respiratory, cardiovascular, anti-diabetic, anti-infective, gastrointestinal, central nervous system, and 
women’s health. Lupin has 15 state-of-the-art manufacturing sites and 6 research centers globally, along with a

During the quarter ended and six months ended September 30, 2026, the Company has determined that the carrying value of 
investment in a subsidiary is higher than the recoverable amount and has provided for diminution in the value of investment of ₹ 769.3 
million.
The Company and its subsidiary are exposed to multiple civil lawsuits alleging anticompetitive behavior related to certain products and a
possible violation of federal and state antitrust laws.These lawsuits were combined into the collection of similar cases referred to as In
Re Generic Pharmaceuticals Antitrust Litigation. Such litigation are often resolved through settlement agreements. During the year
ended March 31 2026, the Company on best estimate recorded a provision of ₹ 4,493.9 million (USD 50.0 million) towards this litigation
without admission of liability or wrongdoing. During the quarter ended March 31, 2026, this provision has been recorded by the
subsidiary and consequently reversed in the standalone results. During the period ended September 30, 2026, the wholly owned
subsidiary settled one of the ongoing antitrust matters for an amount of ₹ 3,162.8 million (USD 35.8 million) without admission of liability
or wrongdoing.
On February 09, 2026, Lupin Limited and its subsidiary entered into a settlement agreement with Astellas towards ongoing dispute
related to Mirabegron ER Tablets a generic version of Myrbetriq ER Tablets in US markets and agreed to pay USD 90.0 million. During
the year ended March 31, 2026, the Company has compensated Lupin Pharmaceuticals, Inc., U.S.A., for the settlement payment of ₹
1,364.7 million (USD 15.0 million) made by it and accordingly expensed. The balance amount of USD 75.0 million towards prepaid
option has been paid and capitalised by the subsidiary.
The Government of India has consolidated 29 existing labour legislations into a unified framework comprising four labour codes as
follows: Code on Wages, 2019, Code on Social Security, 2020, Industrial Relations Code, 2020 and Occupational Safety, Health and
Working Conditions Code, 2020 (collectively referred to as the "New Labour Codes"). The New Labour Codes are effective from
November 21, 2025 and introduce changes that include, among other things, setting a uniform definition of wages. The Company has
assessed the implications of the New Labour Codes and has recognized an incremental cost of ₹ 496.4 million during the year ended
March 31, 2026.
During the previous periods ended September 30, 2025 and March 31, 2026, the Company transferred its Over the Counter ('OTC') and
API R&D business in India to its wholly owned subsidiaries Lupinlife Consumer Healthcare Limited and Lupin Manufacturing Solutions
Limited respectively, as a going concern on slump sale basis for a consideration of ₹ 8,200.0 million and ₹ 180.0 million resulting in gain
on divestment of ₹ 6,589.6 million and ₹ 37.2 million respectively.

As approved by the Members of the Company at the 44th Annual General Meeting held on August 04, 2026, the Company has disbursed on

During the quarter ended September 30, 2026, 57,436 (year to date 110,861) equity shares of ₹ 2/- each, fully paid-up, were allotted upon exercise of the
vested stock options pursuant to the Lupin Employees Stock Option Plans (ESOPs), resulting in an increase in the paid-up equity share capital by ₹ 0.1
million (year to date ₹ 0.2 million) and securities premium account by ₹ 87.1 million (year to date ₹ 164.0 million).
Effective April 01, 2026, Nanomi B.V., Netherlands, a wholly owned subsidiary has acquired the entire share capital of VISUfarma B.V., Netherlands for a
total consideration of ₹ 20,902.7 million (Euro 192.8 million). Fair value of intangibles acquired ₹16,730.2 million, deferred tax liability ₹ 4,182.5 million,
Goodwill ₹ 6,549.4 million has been provisionally accounted based on report of independent valuer. The acquisition related costs are accounted in "Other
expenses".
Effective April 02, 2025, the Company through its wholly owned step-down subsidiary, Lupin Healthcare (UK) Limited, U.K., acquired 100% equity share
capital of Renascience Pharma Limited, U.K., for a consideration of ₹ 1,361.6 million (GBP 12.3 million). Fair value of intangibles acquired ₹ 1,239.4 million,
deferred tax liability ₹ 309.8 million, Goodwill ₹ 325.9 million has been accounted based on report of independent valuer.
During the quarter ended September 30, 2026 and year ended March 31, 2026, the Group has recognised an impairment charge of ₹ 246.8 million and ₹
1,130.1 million respectively related to certain capital work-in-progress, intangible assets and intangible assets under development.
Effective July 01, 2026, Nanomi B.V., Netherlands, increased its ownership interest in Multicare Pharmaceuticals Philippines Inc. (MPPI) from 56.28% to
99.89% through the acquisition of shares from certain existing shareholders for a consideration amounting to ₹ 3,701.2 million and a share buyback
amounting to ₹ 17.0 million.
Effective July 20, 2026, the Company through its wholly owned step-down subsidiary, Lupin Inc., U.S.A., sublicensed two intellectual property assets to
Kaveri Therapeutics Inc., U.S.A. ("Kaveri") in exchange for equity shares valued at ₹ 153.3 million (USD 1.6 million), resulting in an 82.17% ownership
interest. Consequently, Lupin Inc. obtained control over Kaveri, and Kaveri is accounted for as a subsidiary.

The Company and its subsidiary are exposed to multiple civil lawsuits alleging anticompetitive behavior related to certain products and a
possible violation of federal and state antitrust laws.These lawsuits were combined into the collection of similar cases referred to as In
Re Generic Pharmaceuticals Antitrust Litigation. Such litigation are often resolved through settlement agreements. During the year
ended March 31 2026, the Company on best estimate recorded a provision of ₹ 4,493.9 million (USD 50.0 million) towards this litigation
without admission of liability or wrongdoing. During the quarter ended March 31, 2026, this provision has been recorded by the
subsidiary and consequently reversed in the standalone results. During the period ended September 30, 2026, the wholly owned
subsidiary settled one of the ongoing antitrust matters for an amount of ₹ 3,162.8 million (USD 35.8 million) without admission of liability
or wrongdoing.
On February 09, 2026, Lupin Limited and its subsidiary entered into a settlement agreement with Astellas towards ongoing dispute
related to Mirabegron ER Tablets a generic version of Myrbetriq ER Tablets in US markets and agreed to pay USD 90.0 million. During
the year ended March 31, 2026, the Company has compensated Lupin Pharmaceuticals, Inc., U.S.A., for the settlement payment of ₹
1,364.7 million (USD 15.0 million) made by it and accordingly expensed. The balance amount of USD 75.0 million towards prepaid
option has been paid and capitalised by the subsidiary.
The Government of India has consolidated 29 existing labour legislations into a unified framework comprising four labour codes as
follows: Code on Wages, 2019, Code on Social Security, 2020, Industrial Relations Code, 2020 and Occupational Safety, Health and
Working Conditions Code, 2020 (collectively referred to as the "New Labour Codes"). The New Labour Codes are effective from
November 21, 2025 and introduce changes that include, among other things, setting a uniform definition of wages. The Company has
assessed the implications of the New Labour Codes and has recognized an incremental cost of ₹ 496.4 million during the year ended
March 31, 2026.
During the previous periods ended September 30, 2025 and March 31, 2026, the Company transferred its Over the Counter ('OTC') and
API R&D business in India to its wholly owned subsidiaries Lupinlife Consumer Healthcare Limited and Lupin Manufacturing Solutions
Limited respectively, as a going concern on slump sale basis for a consideration of ₹ 8,200.0 million and ₹ 180.0 million resulting in gain
on divestment of ₹ 6,589.6 million and ₹ 37.2 million respectively.
